analysis.one_liner: Guts bank reporting rules, requires warrants for financial records, bans a digital dollar, and lets Congress kill financial regulations.
analysis.headline: One sponsor, zero cosponsors: the bill has sat in five House committees with no action since its March 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules on government access to Americans' financial information. It would require police to get a search warrant before pulling your bank records, end routine reports banks file about transactions like transfers over $10,000, scrap the $600 tax-reporting threshold for online payment platforms, ban the Federal Reserve from issuing a digital dollar, and stop federal agencies from restricting self-hosted crypto wallets. It would also terminate the stock market's Consolidated Audit Trail and require Congress to affirmatively vote to approve most new — and eventually existing — rules from financial regulators, or the rules die.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people gain financial privacy protections: police would need a warrant to access bank records, unauthorized government snooping would carry criminal and civil penalties, and casual online sellers would stop receiving tax forms for small payment volumes. Banks and other financial institutions gain relief from costly anti-money-laundering reporting obligations. Crypto users gain protection for self-hosted wallets and freedom from any future digital dollar.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers seeking financial privacy, banks, crypto users

how_it_helps.text: The bill generally prohibits federal agencies from accessing an individual's financial records without a warrant based on probable cause, and adds criminal penalties (up to 5 years) and civil penalties (at least $1,000 per violation per day) for obtaining or disclosing records unlawfully.
It eliminates requirements that financial institutions report certain transactions to federal agencies; records of such transactions could be obtained only through a search warrant.

It raises the tax-reporting threshold for third-party payment platforms back to $20,000 and 200 transactions per year, undoing the $600 threshold that took effect after the American Rescue Plan, with the change applied retroactively to 2021.

It bans any federal agency or Federal Reserve bank from issuing a central bank digital currency directly to individuals and prohibits agencies from restricting a person's use of convertible virtual currency through a self-hosted wallet.

It requires congressional approval before major rules from financial regulators (the Fed, SEC, CFTC, FDIC, CFPB, Treasury, and NCUA) can take effect, and over five years sunsets existing rules unless Congress votes to approve them.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement and national security agencies lose routine access to bank transaction reports used to detect money laundering, terrorism financing, and tax evasion. Financial regulators would lose much of their practical power, since rules take effect only if Congress affirmatively votes to approve them — something Congress historically rarely does. Market regulators lose the Consolidated Audit Trail, the database used to reconstruct and police trading activity across exchanges.

drawbacks.text: Financial institutions would no longer have to report large cash transactions or suspicious activity; the CRS summary notes these reports exist to detect illicit activity such as money laundering or terrorism financing, and the bill would strip away much of that reporting, including requirements on beneficial ownership of companies and reports from cash-intensive businesses.

The REINS-style provision would let existing financial rules lapse unless Congress affirmatively votes to reapprove them within 90 days of designation — a bar Congress almost never clears, meaning consumer protections, bank safety rules, and anti-fraud rules from financial agencies could quietly expire without any vote being taken on them.

The bill terminates the Consolidated Audit Trail and requires the entities running it to refund all collected fees, removing the centralized record of securities trading that regulators use to reconstruct market events and detect manipulation, and barring any similar database without a new act of Congress.

The government would have to rely solely on search warrants to access financial records, which supporters call a Fourth Amendment safeguard and critics say would slow or block routine financial investigations, including inquiries short of a criminal case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections for individuals — warrant requirements for bank records, penalties for unauthorized disclosure, and an end to $600 tax forms for casual sellers — are real gains for ordinary people, and the crypto and digital-dollar provisions address legitimate surveillance concerns. But the bill goes much further than privacy: it dismantles much of the anti-money-laundering regime, hands financial agencies' rulemaking power to a Congress that must affirmatively approve every major rule or the rule dies, and kills the stock market's audit trail. The practical effect would be to sharply shrink the government's ability to detect financial crime and police market manipulation while giving banks and sophisticated financial actors substantial relief from oversight. The parts are not all priced honestly against each other.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, picked up no cosponsors, and has had no hearings, markups, or votes since — so it just sits there while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Andrew Ogles introduced the bill on March 14, 2025, and it was referred to the Committees on Financial Services, Judiciary, Rules, Budget, and Ways and Means for consideration of the provisions under each committee's jurisdiction.
No cosponsors have joined the bill.
The action history shows no further steps after the initial referrals — no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill stalled, the current reporting regime and financial regulations stay in force, so law enforcement and regulators keep their existing tools; the banks, crypto firms, and others who would benefit from the bill's rollbacks have gotten nothing so far.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators and law enforcement, for now

for.name: Rep. Andrew Ogles
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would gut bank reporting rules, require warrants for financial records, ban a digital dollar, and subject financial regulators' rules to congressional approval.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors of either party and no votes, so no partisan breakdown exists; the bill is a one-member effort that has not advanced.

industries.note: The bill eliminates most Bank Secrecy Act reporting duties, lifting costly compliance obligations, but the same reports are what help detect fraud, money laundering, and illicit finance that harm ordinary customers. Banks would keep their records out of government reach without warrants.

The bill bans any central bank digital currency and bars agencies from restricting purchases through self-hosted wallets, protecting users' ability to hold and spend crypto without government gatekeepers.

industries.industry: Securities trading firms and market participants
industries.note: Terminating the Consolidated Audit Trail ends the centralized record of every stock order, freeing traders from reporting and oversight that regulators use to catch manipulation.

industries.industry: Third-party payment platforms and gig-economy sellers
industries.note: Restoring the $20,000/200-transaction reporting threshold spares platforms from issuing 1099-K forms and spares casual sellers from tax paperwork on small volumes.
Eliminating reporting requirements, beneficial ownership rules, and the audit trail removes demand for the surveillance and recordkeeping systems these firms build for banks and brokerages.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no action in any of five committees for months, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or vote this Congress unless its privacy provisions are folded into a broader vehicle; bills in this position typically expire when the Congress ends.
